blocks.prompt: 18 (i) On Defense Day, Teacher I prepares a list of 10 national songs, and Teacher II also prepares a separate list of 10 different national songs. The principal wants to select 3 songs from Teacher I's list and 3 songs from Teacher II's list. In how many ways can the songs be selected if: (i) The sequence of the selected songs matters
blocks.explanation:
Two separate choices: 3 songs from list I and 3 from list II. "Sequence matters" (as in the book's answer) means the order of the 3 songs taken from each list counts.
Plan: \({}^{10}P_{3} \times {}^{10}P_{3}\).
steps:
Given: two lists of 10 different songs; 3 songs from each list; order matters.
To find: the number of ways.
Method: Ordered choice without repetition from each list is \({}^{10}P_{3}\); both choices are made together, so multiply.

Ordered choices from one list
\[{}^{10}P_{3} = 10 \times 9 \times 8\]
\[= 720\]
Why: First song 10 choices, second 9, third 8.

Multiply for the two lists
\[720 \times 720 = 518400\]
Why: Each ordered choice from list I goes with each ordered choice from list II.

Check
\[{}^{10}P_{3} = {}^{10}C_{3} \times 3! = 120 \times 6 = 720\]
\[720^{2} = 518400 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Each group of 3 songs can be ordered in \(3!\) ways.

blocks.prompt: 18 (ii) On Defense Day, Teacher I prepares a list of 10 national songs, and Teacher II also prepares a separate list of 10 different national songs. The principal wants to select 3 songs from Teacher I's list and 3 songs from Teacher II's list. In how many ways can the songs be selected if: (ii) The sequence of the selected songs does not matter.
blocks.explanation:
Now only which songs are picked counts.
Plan: \({}^{10}C_{3} \times {}^{10}C_{3}\).
steps:
Given: two lists of 10 songs; 3 from each; order does not matter.
To find: the number of ways.
Method: A selection from each list is \({}^{10}C_{3}\); multiply for the two lists.

Selections from one list
\[{}^{10}C_{3} = \dfrac{10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8}{3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1}\]
\[= \dfrac{720}{6} = 120\]
Why: Each group of 3 songs was counted \(3! = 6\) times in \({}^{10}P_{3}\).

Multiply for the two lists
\[120 \times 120 = 14400\]
Why: Each selection from list I goes with each selection from list II.

Check
\[\dfrac{518400}{6 \times 6} = \dfrac{518400}{36} = 14400 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Removing the \(3!\) orders from each list in part (i) gives this part.
